reading.title: The Creek Behind the School
reading.purpose: Follow a fifth-grade class as they find out why their creek is in trouble and help it recover.
paras: Every Friday, Mr. Okafor's fifth graders walked to the creek behind their school to check its health. Lately something was wrong. The tadpoles had begun to dwindle, and last week Jada counted only four.

Upstream, a neighbor was washing cars and letting soapy water run into the creek. "That will pollute the water," said Mr. Okafor. "The soap and oil will contaminate the pond where the tadpoles live, so they cannot eat or breathe safely." The class wrote a polite letter, and the neighbor agreed to wash cars on the lawn.
The class also noticed that the bank was crumbling. Heavy rain had washed away loose soil, a change called erosion. So they planted grass and shrubs whose roots held the dirt in place.

Back at school, the class kept a compost bin. Banana peels and dead leaves began to decompose, breaking down into dark, crumbly soil. "Those peels give back nutrients, the things plants need to grow," said Mr. Okafor. The class spread the compost on the school garden, and the soil became fertile enough to grow tomatoes.

By June, the creek looked healthier. One morning a hawk, a predator that hunts smaller animals, perched on a fence by the garden. A mouse, its prey, hid under a squash leaf. "Everything is connected," Jada whispered. "When the water and soil are healthy, more animals can flourish."

qs.q: In paragraph 4, the word "decompose" means to
choices: wash away from the garden in heavy rain
dry out and turn into hard, dusty lumps
break down slowly into simpler parts
grow bigger when the weather gets warm
qs.why: The peels and leaves decompose by "breaking down into dark, crumbly soil."

qs.q: Which sentence shows how the class slowed the crumbling of the creek bank?
choices: The class wrote a polite letter, and the neighbor agreed to wash cars on the lawn.
So they planted grass and shrubs whose roots held the dirt in place.
Banana peels and dead leaves began to decompose, breaking down into dark, crumbly soil.
Every Friday, Mr. Okafor's fifth graders walked to the creek behind their school to check its health.
qs.why: Roots hold soil, so planting grass and shrubs keeps the bank from washing away.

ev.text: So they planted grass and shrubs whose roots held the dirt in place.

qs.q: Why did the number of tadpoles most likely dwindle?
choices: Soapy, oily water made their pond unsafe to live in.
Hungry hawks had hunted most of them from the fence.
Heavy rain had pushed all of the tadpoles out to sea.
The class had moved them to a tank inside the school.
qs.why: Mr. Okafor says soap and oil will contaminate the pond, so the tadpoles cannot eat or breathe safely.

qs.q: What is the main idea of this story?
choices: Hawks and mice are the most important animals near a school.
A neighbor should never be asked to change anything he does.
Compost is the only way to make a school garden grow well.
Caring for water and soil helps living things stay healthy.
qs.why: The class fixes the water, the bank, and the soil, and the last paragraph says healthy water and soil help more animals flourish.

clues.text: breaking down into dark, crumbly soil
the things plants need to grow
